summary:
Bursa stands under the national framework of Türkiye, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, together with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and would punish taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years in prison. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. The draft had not been passed when reported, yet authorities have acted as though its prohibitions were already in force.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and impose a mandatory permanent-infertility condition, exposing health professionals who provide such care to penalties. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the measure. A separate Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option on gender-reassignment medical-board reports and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, "A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned Into State Policy", presented at its launch by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, finds that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy during the year. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The government frames its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals".

Street-level enforcement reaches visitors directly. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, and Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Detention compounds the risk. Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities: the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer, and no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners.
tangentialFactors:
Pride events remain flashpoints across the country. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The pending status of the draft package is itself a source of turbulence. The measure had not been enacted when reported in October 2025, but the gap between text and statute has not constrained enforcement, and the reported pattern is of authorities applying prohibitions before they exist in law.

The depth of the regime predates the current government's legislative programme. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the pattern's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Contested framing surrounds the care restrictions. Online discussion of the Health Ministry regulation was cast as an "LGBT opening", a characterisation rights groups reject, and the Turkish Medical Association's opposition to the draft places the national medical establishment against the government's position.
localsOnly:
Residents face exposure under a draft that would criminalise conduct and advocacy directly. Penalties reported against health professionals and patients under the gender-affirming-care provisions apply to people living in the country, not only to visitors, and the age threshold of 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate would reshape what care is available domestically.

Documentation of violations is concentrated in civil society. Kaos GL's annual reporting, the Truth Justice Memory Center's Pride monitoring, and coordinated statements from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın are the channels through which incidents are recorded and demands for investigation are made.

Custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers in the Sincan case reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

Complaint mechanisms inside the prison system are ineffective and can attract further violence. Transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, and complaints offer little protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bursa-specific incident, detention, Pride or policing data appears in the source inventory for this record. The findings above are drawn from national reporting and from incidents in other cities, and are presented as the framework a visitor to Bursa stands under rather than as documented events in Bursa itself.

Whether GBT-style identity stops of the kind recorded in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district occur in Bursa is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The current legislative status of the 11th Judicial Package after October 2025 is unresolved in the inventory. The draft was reported as pending and not yet passed; whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is not sourced.

The inventory does not state whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation applies uniformly to every province or allows provincial variation beyond the Kayseri circular cited.

The claim that foreign visitors must produce original identity documents at transit checkpoints rests on general reporting on passport-carrying rules; the inventory does not document a Bursa-specific checkpoint practice or the frequency of document checks in that city.
